newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Ratings key as EMU reduces currency risk.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ratings key as EMU reduces currency risk.

text.p: By Jacqueline Thorpe,
If a single European currency achieves one of its main objectives, it will eliminate costly and disturbing currency fluctuations.
But it will also eliminate a country's ability to print money, a method of last resort in paying back debt.
That, say analysts, is at the heart of discussion over credit ratings under European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
As the European Central Bank (ECB) takes over from individual institutions and the power to print money disappears, will countries be able to maintain their current debt ratings?
Or was that only a theoretical safety valve to begin with?
Rating agencies such as Standard & Poor's, Moody's Investors Service and IBCA will need to look even more closely at a country's fiscal health to answer that question, analysts say.
Apart from debt, deficits and budgets, broader issues such as labour markets, tax structure, and pension funding will come under closer scrutiny.
While ratings of some countries may come under pressure, corporate ratings could benefit as credit ratings take on vital importance after EMU starting in 1999.
"Credit is going to be the number one issue in terms of European bonds," said Michael Lewis, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
CORE COUNTRY RATINGS SET TO STAND
IBCA, the European credit rating agency, and Standard & Poor's have said the credit quality of sovereign countries joining EMU would likely remain strong.
Moody's has not released an official preview of its plans for ratings after EMU.

Foreign and local debt issued by Germany, France, the Netherlands, Austria and Luxembourg, likely candidates for EMU in the first wave, are all rated AAA by the major rating agencies and that is unlikely to change.
The whole EMU-area is also likely to receive an AAA rating which will act as a ceiling for debt ratings within that area. Each country would also be individually rated.

"If you form a European monetary union there would be a single ceiling for that entire area which would likely be AAA, given the membership and the strength of the overall economic area," David Levey, co-head of sovereign ratings for Moody's.
BELGIUM, IRELAND, FINLAND RATINGS AT RISK
However, the ratings of Belgium, Ireland and Finland, three potential EMU candidates, could be eroded.
These three countries currently have AAA local currency ratings but lower ratings for their foreign currency debt.
IBCA has said that without the ability to print money, the ratings of these countries would probably drift down to the level of their foreign currency ratings.

Lewis at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said ratings for both Ireland and Finland would be at risk because their two main trading partners -- Britain and Sweden respectively -- will likely remain outside the EMU block at the beginning, increasing the risk of secession.
Belgium could suffer because it has a huge amount of debt set to be converted into euros, he said.
CREDIT RISK ALREADY REFLECTED IN THE MARKETS
Analysts said credit risk of sovereign debt, minus currency risk, can be assessed by looking at yields of sovereign Eurobonds over benchmark German Bunds.
Yields on mark Eurobonds issued by countries such as Belgium, Finland and Italy currently trade over Bunds.

For example, a Belgian Eurobond maturing in May, 2002 is currently quoted around 26 basis points over comparable German government paper, a Finnish February 2003 Eurobond was quoted 11 basis points over, and Spain's 10-year mark Eurobond launched on December 5 was priced to yield 24 basis points over Bunds.
"This is credit risk only, with currency risk stripped out," said Deutsche's Lewis. "And you can see the differences."
RATINGS FOR COUNTRIES OUTSIDE EMU SHOULD STAND
While Belgium, Ireland and Finland may see their credit ratings slip, countries outside EMU like Britain should be able to hang onto theirs on the basis of their sound economics.

"Britain won't be at risk for a downgrade," said Bronwyn Curtis, chief economist at Nomura Research Institute in London. "They have done a lot more than other countries in terms of deregulation, pensions and getting their fiscal situation under control," she said.
Italy and Spain, which may not make it into the first wave, should also be able to retain high ratings as they struggle to get into shape for the second round, analysts say.
"Unless of course they abandon all hope and start pursuing irresponsible policies," said Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW in London. "And that very is unlikely."
RATING ANALYSIS TO BECOME MORE DETAILED
Analysts and rating agencies said whether ratings stand or fall, agencies will need to look deeper at the mechanics of a country's economy to assess credit risk after EMU.
While the whole process of EMU has been broadly positive for ratings as countries slash spending and deficits to meet the strict criteria for entry, it has also produced unpleasant side effects.
High unemployment, a feature of Germany and France in the run-up to EMU, can put pressure on deficits as governments pay out more in social security benefits.
Whether countries can maintain austere economic policy after EMU will be critical as well.

Levey at Moody's said the rating agency would be looking closely at the consequences of not having an exchange rate mechanism as a form of adjustment and the role of the ECB in setting monetary policy.
"What degree of flexibility would they lose and what would they gain?," said Levey. "Printing money -- was it anything more than a theoretical possibility?"
Lewis said tax structure would be a major focus for agencies as taxation replaces printing money as means of raising funds to repay obligations.
Countries can raise taxes but there will come a point where corporations will shirk high duties for more tax-friendly climates.
"It's going to be a competition as to which country sets the lowest taxes in Europe," Lewis said.
CORPORATE RATINGS LIKELY TO PROFIT
Investors may be pleasantly surpised by the effect of EMU on corporate ratings, agencies and analysts said.
S&P said EMU should be broadly positive for credit trends within Euorpean countries without triggering substantial changes for corporate ratings.

"The most straightforward benefits of a single currency stem from the reduction in cross-border financial transaction costs within the EMU zone, via the elimination of foreign exchange risks and costs," said Rupert Atkinson, director of corporate ratings for S&P, in a report.
While one-off costs of switching to the euro may depress profitabliltiy inititally, the cost of capital should be reduced by low interest and inflation rates.
A fiscally sound corporation could even be in the unusual position of having a higher credit rating than its home country, as an AAA euro rating becomes its ceiling, analysts said.
"Corporates will be nearly as important as sovereigns," said Curtis.
